title: The Prepared Foods Supply Chain Is a Different Animal Than Center Store
summary: Prepared foods runs on a different supply chain than center store. See what suppliers need for item data, replenishment, and allergen rules.
body_markdown:
In this article, learn about:


-


Why replenishment cycles in the deli case run on days instead of weeks


-


What a menu refresh actually costs a supplier in item setup work


-


The allergen and traceability dates that now apply to grab-and-go items


-


How suppliers get ready to scale in[grocery and food service](https://www.spscommerce.com/industries/grocery-food-services/)


Shoppers now treat the deli case as a restaurant substitute. In a 2025 FMI survey of 1,571 grocery shoppers,[28% said they buy deli-prepared foods instead of going to a restaurant, up from 12% in 2017](https://www.grocerydive.com/news/deli-prepared-foods-grocery-foodservice-restaurants/802478/) . Retail foodservice sales reached $52.1 billion over the 52 weeks that ended Aug. 9, 2025, according to NielsenIQ data that FMI cited.


Grocers have responded by investing in the category. That means onboarding more suppliers to fill it, such as regional commissaries, local food manufacturers, and co-packers. They are often the least integrated vendors a grocer works with.


This is where the trouble starts. Prepared foods runs on a different supply chain than center store (the shelf-stable, ambient grocery aisles), even though it moves through the same purchase order. Its shorter date codes mean tighter delivery windows and less room for error. The failures it produces look like execution problems, but they are usually data problems.


## Why Is the Prepared Foods Supply Chain Different From Center Store?


Prepared foods differs from center store in three ways: how fast it moves, how often its items change, and what its product data has to carry. A supplier who scales into the category on center-store processes meets all three at once.


Attribute


Center store


Prepared foods


Replenishment cycle


Weeks of supply


Days, sometimes a single day


Item churn


Stable assortment, periodic resets


Continuous creation and teardown


Attribute requirements


Standard product data


Allergen, ingredient, and nutrition data with regulatory weight


Shelf life


Months to years


Days


Failure mode


Stockout


Shrink, then a scorecard penalty


The last row is the one that surprises suppliers. In center store, a late shipment leaves a gap that the next delivery fills. In prepared foods, product that arrives late or gets ordered wrong is often product that gets thrown away.


## How Does Fresh Food Replenishment Change the Forecast?


Fresh food replenishment leaves almost no buffer between the forecast and the delivery. A shelf-stable supplier plans in weeks of supply. If the forecast misses, inventory absorbs it. In contrast, a prepared foods supplier produces against orders that land days before the product has to be on the shelf, and the product is unsellable within a week.


Two things follow. First, item data has to be right before the order arrives, because there is no time to fix it after. When the purchase order and the receiving system disagree, the delivery gets rejected or short-received, and the product expires.


Second, performance measurement gets tighter. Grocers score fresh vendors on the same on-time and in-full measures they use elsewhere, but they tolerate far less. One large grocery retailer working with SPS Commerce[increased on-time performance by 4 to 8% and cut late ship violations by 52%](https://www.spscommerce.com/resources/case-study-grocery-scpm/) after moving to shared vendor visibility. The case study is anonymized and covers the grocer’s whole vendor base, not prepared foods alone. It still shows what the scorecard pressure looks like from the retailer side.


**Related Reading:**[How To Avoid Common Shipping Errors](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/how-to-avoid-common-shipping-errors)


## Why Does Deli Item Data Management Never Stop?


Deli item data management is a standing load, not a one-time onboarding project, because the assortment never settles. Menus refresh with the season, with local demand, and with whatever the category buyer wants to test next. Each refresh creates work that has to clear the retailer’s validation before the item can be ordered.


### What Each Menu Refresh Requires


A new or reformulated item generally needs:


-


A new Global Trade Item Number (GTIN), along with the case and pack configuration that goes with it


-


A complete attribute set, including ingredients, allergens, and nutrition values


-


A revised nutrition panel when the formulation changes


-


Product images that meet the retailer’s specification


-


Retailer-side validation, which can reject the item and send it back for correction


A supplier with a stable center-store assortment does this work once and then maintains it, while a prepared foods supplier repeats it every few weeks, for every banner they sell into. Each banner has its own portal and its own validation rules. Suppliers with no one clearly responsible for item data feel this first, because the work has no owner until something gets rejected.


**Related Reading:**[Why Item Setup Matters: A Guide for New Retail Suppliers](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/why-item-setup-matters-a-guide-for-new-retail-suppliers)


## What Are the New Grocery Allergen Labeling Requirements?


Two dates matter for suppliers making grab-and-go items, and both come from regulators rather than retailers.


-


**New York, November 12, 2026.**[Section 199-G of the New York Agriculture and Markets Law](https://newyork.public.law/laws/n.y._agriculture_and_markets_law_section_199-g) requires food establishments to label prepackaged food with written notice of any major food allergen it contains. The statute defines prepackaged food as food prepared, prepacked, and sold on the same premises. It excludes food packaged after a customer orders it, and names nine major allergens: milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, wheat, peanuts, sesame, and soybeans.


-


**FSMA 204, July 20, 2028.** The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) rule on[additional traceability records for certain foods](https://www.fda.gov/food/food-safety-modernization-act-fsma/fsma-final-rule-requirements-additional-traceability-records-certain-foods) covers items on the Food Traceability List, which includes ready-to-eat deli salads. The compliance date moved to July 20, 2028 in a[Federal Register notice published Aug. 7, 2025](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/08/07/2025-14967/requirements-for-additional-traceability-records-for-certain-foods-compliance-date-extension) . Several vendor summaries still print the older January 2026 date, so it is worth checking the primary source.


Both dates ask the same thing of a supplier. Attribute data has to exist for each item, stay current as formulations change, and travel in a form the buyer can receive. That is a different job than printing a label.


## Why Is Commissary Supplier Onboarding the Pressure Point?


Commissary supplier onboarding is where the demand growth and the integration gap meet. Grocers expanding prepared foods are adding vendors from the least integrated part of their supplier base. Both sides have a fair position.


The grocer needs speed. A category that refreshes every six weeks can’t wait months for a vendor to become orderable, and the buyer is measured on filling the case. The supplier often has no electronic data interchange (EDI) capability and no one who owns item data. Asking a 40-person commissary to stand that up on a buyer’s timeline takes real investment.


Distributors hit the same problem at scale. Gordon Food Service works with more than 3,500 suppliers, and bringing one onto EDI took months, because suppliers varied so widely in size and technical skill. Working with SPS Commerce, the company[cut supplier EDI onboarding time from months to weeks](https://www.spscommerce.com/resources/gordon-foods/) and improved its readiness for FSMA 204 recordkeeping. Gordon is a foodservice distributor, not a prepared foods maker, so the parallel is directional. The bottleneck it describes is the same one grocers hit in the deli case.


**Related Reading:**[Grocery Supply Chain Issues: 3 Pressures Reshaping 2026](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/grocery-supply-chain-issues-3-pressures-reshaping-2026)


## What Does “Ready” Look Like for a Prepared Foods Supplier?


Suppliers who scale in this category tend to have the same things in place before the volume arrives. A short self-assessment:


-


One named owner for item data, with authority across every banner the company sells into


-


An item setup process that runs on a regular cadence, not as a project each time


-


Full allergen, ingredient, and nutrition data for each item, updated when a recipe changes


-


EDI orders and shipping documents with each retailer, including[advance ship notices](https://www.spscommerce.com/edi-document/edi-856-advance-shipping-notice/) that match what arrives at the dock


-


A view of the retailer’s scorecard, current enough to catch a pattern before it becomes a penalty


-


A documented path for how a new item goes from kitchen to orderable, and how long that takes


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What counts as prepared foods in a grocery store?


Prepared foods generally covers items made ready to eat or ready to heat and sold in the deli, bakery, or grab-and-go case. That includes hot bar and salad bar items, sandwiches, rotisserie proteins, packaged meals, and deli salads. Suppliers include in-store production, regional commissaries, local manufacturers, and co-packers.


### How is prepared foods replenishment different from center store?


Center store plans in weeks of supply against a stable assortment. Prepared foods plans in days, against items that expire within a week. A forecast miss shows up as thrown-away product, not as an empty shelf that the next delivery fills.


### Does the New York allergen law apply to every prepared item?


It applies to prepackaged food, which the statute defines as food prepared, prepacked, and sold on the same premises. Food packaged after a customer orders it is excluded. How the definition lands on a specific item is a question for a compliance team or counsel.


### What does a grocer look at when deciding whether a prepared foods supplier can scale?


Buyers tend to look at three things: how fast a supplier can get a new item orderable, how complete and current the item attributes are, and how the supplier performs on on-time and in-full measures once volume starts.
